questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: say what a label contributes that an unlabelled row cannot
questions.stem: A team holds 40,000 cases each marked fraudulent or legitimate, and it also holds 900,000 unmarked cases from the same source. What distinguishes the two collections?

options.text: The marked cases carry the answer with them, and they are the only ones that can show a model what right looks like
The marked cases are simply the first 40,000 drawn, and the marks record which team happened to look at each
options.misconception: believes a label is a record of provenance rather than of an outcome

options.text: The unmarked cases are the more valuable of the two, since the shape of a population can be learned with no answers at all
options.misconception: claims that structure alone substitutes for knowing the outcome

options.text: Neither collection carries an answer, since the marks are opinions and the unmarked cases are measurements rather than judgements
options.misconception: assumes measured features are more objective than an outcome label

questions.explanation: A label is the one piece of information that turns an observation into a question with a checkable answer, and it is what lets a fit be scored rather than merely performed. The 900,000 unmarked cases are far more numerous and genuinely useful, but everything a supervised method learns from them is borrowed structure: the clusters, the densities and the directions of variation are all discovered without ever being told which outcome goes with which case. That is why the labelled set is the scarce resource rather than the large one, and why the usual first question about a new problem is not how much data there is but how much of it has an answer attached.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two collections could tell a method whether it was right.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: explain why regression and classification need different losses
questions.stem: One model predicts a delivery time in hours and another predicts whether a parcel arrives late. What has changed about the thing being predicted, and what follows from it?

options.text: One target is a quantity where a distance means something and the other is a label with no middle, so the losses differ in kind
Only the units differ, since both are predictions against a recorded outcome and one loss serves either equally well
options.misconception: believes a shared loss is adequate once the two targets are on a common scale

options.text: The first is the harder question, because a continuous target simply carries more information than a category does
options.misconception: assumes a continuous target makes a problem harder rather than differently shaped

options.text: Nothing structural differs, and the only requirement is that the loss be applied to whichever column the data happens to hold
options.misconception: treats the choice of loss as independent of what is being predicted

questions.explanation: A delivery time of 20 hours is two hours away from 22 in a way that means something, so a loss can measure the size of a miss and prefer a near miss to a wild one. Late or not late has no such middle: a model that answers late when the answer was on time is entirely wrong, and no arithmetic on the two labels improves it. That is the whole reason the two problems have separate machinery, since one optimises a distance on a continuous scale and the other optimises a decision on a discrete one, and a model that is asked to regress a label will happily return 0.4 and call it a prediction of a category nobody chose.
questions.hint: Ask whether a value halfway between the two possible answers could ever be a sensible answer.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a squared loss punishes outliers
questions.learningObjective: explain what a large error costs under a squared loss
questions.stem: One model is wrong by one hour on each of three cases and right on all three. A second case is then mispredicted by twenty hours. What does a squared training loss do with that case?

options.text: It charges four hundred for the single miss, so one bad case outweighs a hundred small ones and pulls the fit towards it
It charges twenty, the same as any other miss, because the loss only compares a prediction with its own target
options.misconception: believes the cost of a miss grows in step with the size of the miss

options.text: It charges nothing, since one case cannot move a total that is computed over every case in the training set
options.misconception: believes a total is immune to the size of its individual terms

options.text: It charges four, because the loss takes a square root of the total before comparing it with any other total
options.misconception: believes the loss reduces squared terms before summing them

questions.explanation: Squaring makes the penalty grow faster than the mistake, so a miss of twenty costs four hundred while a miss of one costs one, and that single case outweighs a hundred one-hour errors. A fit minimising this total will therefore spend much of its effort on the row that produced the biggest number, and the effect is not merely a slightly worse fit but a fit shaped around an exceptional case. Whether that is right depends on the world: if twenty hours of error genuinely ruins a parcel while two hours is a nuisance, the quadratic cost is an accurate description of the harm, and if it does not, the same property is a defect. The choice of loss is a claim about costs.
questions.hint: Ask how the cost of a miss changes as the miss gets bigger, and compare a miss of one with a miss of twenty.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why an absolute loss is robust
questions.learningObjective: explain the effect of switching from a squared to an absolute loss
questions.stem: A team replaces a squared regression loss with an absolute one. Which change in the fit follows directly from the swap?

options.text: A single wildly wrong prediction stops dominating the total, since its cost now grows in step with the error itself
The fit becomes more sensitive to the largest errors, because a penalty that grows slowly eventually beats one that grows fast
options.misconception: believes slower growth makes a penalty harsher on big errors

options.text: The fit is unchanged in every case, because the two losses are minimised by the same weights on every dataset
options.misconception: assumes two different losses agree on their minimum for all data

options.text: The fit improves on every target, since the smaller penalty is always the truer measure of what the business loses
options.misconception: conflates a smaller numeric penalty with a better model

questions.explanation: Squaring turns the loss into a system where a few extreme rows set the terms that matter, which is the right behaviour when an extreme error really is far worse and the wrong behaviour when it is a keying mistake or a warehouse fire. An absolute loss charges twenty for a miss of twenty and one for a miss of one, so the fit is determined by the bulk of the cases and a single absurd row cannot drag it. The cost of that robustness is a real one, namely that the absolute loss stops caring about the difference between a small and a middling error within the ordinary range, so the result is a fit to the typical case rather than a careful fit to all of them.
questions.hint: Ask how the penalty compares a miss of one with a miss of twenty under each loss.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: explain how accuracy can rise while a classifier gets less useful
questions.stem: Only four parcels in every hundred in a network arrive late, and a model is being asked to predict lateness. What does reporting one accuracy figure risk?

options.text: Calling every parcel on time scores 0.96 while catching no late parcel at all, so the score can rise as usefulness falls
Accuracy is meaningless at any base rate, so the figure should never be reported whatever the class balance turns out to be
options.misconception: concludes that a metric is useless rather than that it answers one question only

options.text: Accuracy is exactly the right figure here, since 0.96 is a genuine count of how often the model is correct
options.misconception: treats a high correct-case share as proof of a useful model

options.text: Accuracy is safe only when the classes are perfectly balanced, which is the one case in which it is least needed
options.misconception: believes balance is the condition under which accuracy becomes reliable

questions.explanation: Accuracy is a weighted average of the two class rates, weighted by how many rows each class has, so with ninety-six on-time rows the correct answer dominates the total no matter what the model does about the four that matter. A model that never predicts late therefore scores 0.96 while being worth nothing operationally, and a model that finds two of the four late parcels can score lower than that if it costs a false alarm for each. The fix is not to abandon accuracy but to report it beside the two class rates separately, or a summary that weights them equally, so the reader can see which class the headline is being carried by.
questions.hint: Ask what a model that never predicts the rare class scores, and whether that model is worth deploying.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: state what each rate measures and why one can be high alone
questions.stem: A model flags parcels for a manual check, and the team reports both rates: the share of flagged parcels that really are late, and the share of late parcels that get flagged. Why is neither rate enough on its own?

options.text: Each divides by a different group, so a high first rate with a low second can leave most of the late parcels unflagged
Each is a fraction of the same group, so one being high always forces the other high and the two cannot disagree
options.misconception: believes the two rates are two views of a single shared number

options.text: Each ignores the parcels that were not flagged, so neither can tell a useful model from an idle one by itself
options.misconception: attributes the insufficiency of one rate to the wrong group being excluded

options.text: Each is a rate rather than a count, so the two cannot be compared with one another at any base rate at all
options.misconception: believes two rates are incomparable because they are expressed as rates

questions.explanation: The first rate is computed over the flagged group and the second over the group that should have been flagged, so a model can be extremely careful about the small set it does flag while ignoring almost the whole problem. Flag only four parcels a day, get three of them right, and the first rate is 0.75 while the second is 0.01, and a team reading only the first will conclude the model is excellent. The reverse is the other standard failure, a model that flags everything and so catches every late parcel while making its manual check unworkable. Neither rate is wrong and each describes a different decision, which is why a decision about costs is what picks between them.
questions.hint: Ask which group each rate divides by, and construct a model that scores well on one and badly on the other.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What the area under a curve measures
questions.learningObjective: state what an area-under-curve figure does and does not depend on
questions.stem: A team reports an area of 0.71 under a curve of false-positive rate against true-positive rate. What has that figure actually measured about the model?

options.text: How well the model orders its cases, independent of where any decision threshold is finally placed on that order
How many correct decisions it makes at the one threshold its author happened to pick while fitting it
options.misconception: believes the figure is tied to the single threshold used during fitting

options.text: How often it is right on cases from the same population it was fitted on, with that threshold included
options.misconception: reads the figure as a sample accuracy measure

options.text: How well it separates the classes when the threshold is placed so that half of all cases get flagged
options.misconception: assumes the figure presumes one particular fixed-alarm threshold

questions.explanation: The curve is generated by sliding the threshold through every possible value and recording the two rates at each, so the area underneath is a summary of the whole ordering at once rather than of one point on it. A figure of 0.71 therefore says the model puts a genuinely late case above an on-time one more often than chance, and it is comparable between two models without either of them having been given the same alarm level. What it deliberately excludes is the operating point, and that is both its strength and its limitation: a model can have a high area and still be unusable at any threshold that keeps the false alarms affordable, so the number has to be read together with the threshold that will actually be set.
questions.hint: Ask how many thresholds the curve covers, and what the area would be if only one threshold were used.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: predict how the two error counts move when a threshold moves
questions.stem: A scoring model returns one number per case, and a team lowers the value above which a case is flagged. What happens to the two error counts?

options.text: False positives rise and false negatives fall, since lowering the bar draws more cases into the flagged group
Both counts fall, because a lower threshold can only ever be a stricter version of the same test
options.misconception: reads a lower cut-off as a stricter test rather than a looser one

options.text: False positives fall and false negatives rise, because a lower threshold is by definition weaker than the one it replaces
options.misconception: reverses which direction the looser threshold pushes each error count

options.text: Neither count moves, because the counts belong to the score rather than to the place the score is cut
options.misconception: believes the error counts are independent of the operating point

questions.explanation: The threshold decides which side of the line each case falls on, and lowering it moves cases from the unflagged side to the flagged side. On-time parcels swept in by the lower bar become false positives, and late parcels that were previously below the bar become true catches rather than misses, so one count rises while the other falls and the total flagged grows. The score itself does not change at all, which is the reason a threshold is a decision rather than a model improvement: the ranking was fixed when the model was fitted, and moving the cut only chooses which part of that ranking to act on. Anyone who can move a threshold can therefore change a reported rate without changing a single weight.
questions.hint: Ask which cases cross the line when the line moves down, and what each of them becomes.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: state the cost assumption embedded in a single combined score
questions.stem: A team quotes a single combined score of 0.80 for its late-parcel model, computed as the harmonic mean of two rates. What has that one figure assumed about the relative cost of the two kinds of mistake?

options.text: That a false alarm and a missed late parcel are equally worth avoiding, because the harmonic mean weights them equally
That false alarms are the cheaper mistake, because the combined score falls more slowly when one rate rises
options.misconception: reads the shape of the combination as a statement about which error is cheaper

options.text: That missed parcels are the cheaper mistake, because the combined score is always set by whichever rate is smaller
options.misconception: believes the combined score is dominated by whichever rate happens to be lower

options.text: That both costs were measured and combined, so the figure already reflects what the business actually loses
options.misconception: assumes a single combined score can carry a measured cost weighting

questions.explanation: Combining two rates into one requires weighting them, and this combination is defined by taking the harmonic mean, which treats the two as equally important and refuses to let either be rescued by being large. That is a genuine choice rather than a neutral summary, and it is the right one only when a false alarm and a missed parcel cost about the same. When one is many times dearer, the number is being asked a question nobody posed: a model with 0.95 on one rate and 0.60 on the other scores 0.737 here, and the fact that this sits between the two tells you the weighting is even rather than that either is acceptable. The honest alternative is to state the cost ratio and set the threshold accordingly.
questions.hint: Ask what the combination would do if one of the two rates were much more important than the other.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a hyperparameter from a fitted parameter
questions.stem: A team sets the depth of a tree ensemble by hand, and the fitted split thresholds inside it arrive from the data. Which pairing names the two correctly?

options.text: Depth is chosen before fitting and governs the fitting; the split thresholds are estimated from the data during it
Both are parameters, since both end up written into the model and are therefore learned rather than chosen
options.misconception: equates being stored in the model with being estimated from data

options.text: Both are settings, because any number a team looks at before scoring the model counts as chosen by definition
options.misconception: defines the two by when a number is inspected rather than by what produced it

options.text: Depth is a parameter because it is stored in the model, and split thresholds are settings because they sit at each node
options.misconception: classifies the two by where in the model they are written

questions.explanation: The dividing line is not where a number ends up but what produced it. A depth is a decision about the family of models to search, taken before any data is fitted, and the fitting procedure then uses it to decide how many splits to make; a split threshold is a number the data chose, and a different sample would have produced a different one. The confusion is easy because both appear in the saved model and both can be printed, and because a search over depths is itself a fitting procedure, which blurs the vocabulary further. The practical consequence is about what must be refitted: change a setting and the same fitting code runs again, while the parameters come out of the data each time.
questions.hint: Ask what produced each number: a person's decision, or the sample it was fitted on.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: explain what combining many trees actually removes
questions.stem: A random forest grows many trees, each on a resampled copy of the data with a random subset of features considered at each split. What does the forest answer, and why?

options.text: The aggregate of the trees' answers, since averaging many fits cancels the part of each error that came from its sample
The answer of the one tree that saw every row, since only an unresampled tree knows the data reliably
options.misconception: believes the tree fitted on the whole sample is therefore the most accurate

options.text: The average of the feature values rather than of the trees' answers, since the features are what the trees partitioned
options.misconception: confuses averaging the inputs with averaging the models built on them

options.text: The answer of the most frequently selected tree, since the tree chosen most often is the closest to the truth
options.misconception: confuses a summary over trees with picking one representative tree

questions.explanation: Each tree is fitted on a different sample and a different subset of features, so each one's particular mistakes are largely its own, while the signal it captures is present in all of them. Averaging leaves the shared signal and cancels a good share of the unshared error, which is the same reason a crowd of slightly biased estimates can beat one good estimate, and it is why the trees are grown deep and unpruned rather than being individually polished. What averaging cannot remove is error the trees share, which comes from a bias in the model family itself, so a forest of shallow trees remains shallow however many of them there are.
questions.hint: Ask what the trees disagree about and what they agree about, and which of those the aggregate keeps.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: explain what makes boosting sequential rather than an average
questions.stem: A boosting round fits a new model to the cases the current ensemble gets wrong and then adds it in. What makes this different from averaging independent trees?

options.text: Each round's errors are the next round's target, so the rounds depend on one another and an early mistake shapes all that follow
Nothing structural differs, since the trees are still resampled and combined by a weighted vote once the last round is done
options.misconception: assumes resampling plus a final vote is the whole description of either method

options.text: Each round sees a larger sample than the one before, so the final ensemble has been fitted on strictly more data than the first round
options.misconception: believes repeated rounds accumulate additional training data

options.text: Each round is fitted with no resampling at all, and it is that absence which removes the dependence between rounds
options.misconception: attributes the sequential character to the absence of resampling

questions.explanation: In averaging, the trees are fitted in ignorance of one another and the combination is a sum of independent contributions, so nothing one tree finds can change what another is looking for. In boosting, each tree is fitted to the residual errors of what has been built so far, which makes the sequence a conversation: a pattern the early rounds failed on is the one the next round is handed. That is where the extra accuracy comes from, and it is also where the fragility lies, since a mistake in an early round is baked into the target every later round is chasing, which is why a well-chosen learning rate and a limit on the round count matter more here than anywhere else.
questions.hint: Ask what the new model is fitted on, and whether that depends on what came before.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute accuracy from four counts
questions.stem: A confusion matrix built by hand holds 30 true positives, 10 false positives, 5 false negatives and 55 true negatives. What is the accuracy of the model on these 100 cases?
questions.explanation: The correct cases are the 30 genuinely late parcels the model caught plus the 55 on-time parcels it left alone, so 30 + 55 = 85 out of 100, which is 0.85. The independent route is to count the wrong ones instead: 10 + 5 = 15 mistakes out of 100, and 1 − 0.15 = 0.85. The figure is exact and it is also the least informative number on the table, since 55 of the 65 on-time cases make accuracy mostly a statement about the class that was easy, which is why the four counts are worth building by hand even when the headline is a single number.
questions.hint: Add the two correct cells, then divide by the total; confirm by subtracting the two error cells from one.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute precision from two cells of a confusion matrix
questions.stem: From the same hand-built matrix, with 30 true positives and 10 false positives, what is the model's precision over the cases it flagged?
questions.explanation: The flagged group is the 30 true positives plus the 10 false positives, which is 40 cases, and 30 of those 40 are genuine, so precision is 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75. The independent route is the same count described from the other end: the model's 30 correct flags plus its 10 wrong ones are everything it said yes to, and 30 ÷ (30 + 10) returns 0.75. The denominator is the whole point, because it is the flagged group rather than the late group, and using the late group instead would give 0.857, which is a different rate answering a different question about how many late parcels the model managed to reach.
questions.hint: Take the flagged cases as the denominator, not the late cases.

questions.learningObjective: compute recall from two cells of a confusion matrix
questions.stem: From the same hand-built matrix, with 30 true positives and 5 false negatives, what is the model's recall of the parcels that were genuinely late?

questions.topic: A combined score from the counts
questions.learningObjective: compute a combined rate from the cells of a confusion matrix
questions.stem: A model has 30 true positives, 10 false positives and 5 false negatives, which gives precision 0.75 and recall 0.857. What is the combined score computed as the harmonic mean of those two rates?

The independent route goes straight to the counts, where the same combination reduces to twice the true positives over twice the true positives plus the two error cells: 2 × 30 ÷ (2 × 30 + 10 + 5) = 60 ÷ 75 = 0.8. That form is the one worth remembering, because it shows the combined score is really a weighted precision in which the weight is the number of genuine cases, and it is why a model with one rate near one and the other near zero still scores poorly.

questions.topic: The same model on a balanced block
questions.learningObjective: compute how a classifier performs once the class balance changes
questions.stem: A model is fitted on 1,000 parcels of which 100 are late. It finds 90 of the late ones and raises 45 false alarms. The same model, unchanged, is then applied to 1,000 parcels of which 500 are late. Keeping its two class rates as they were, how many of the second block does it classify correctly?
questions.explanation: Its rate on late parcels was 90 ÷ 100 = 0.9, so on 500 late parcels it catches 0.9 × 500 = 450, and its rate on on-time parcels was 855 ÷ 900 = 0.95, so on 500 of those it correctly leaves 0.95 × 500 = 475 alone. Correct classifications are therefore 450 + 475 = 925. The independent route checks the arithmetic against the original block, where the same two rates give 90 + 855 = 945 out of 1,000, so the balanced block is worse by exactly 20, and that fall is caused by nothing but the change in mix. This is why a headline figure from a rare-outcome problem is not transferable, and why the base rate belongs beside any rate at all.
questions.hint: Convert each class rate into a count on the new block, then add the two counts.

The independent route works in rates rather than counts: recall rises from 0.5 to 0.8, a change of 0.3, and 0.3 × 2,000 = 600. The number on its own is not a recommendation, because the same move necessarily sweeps in on-time parcels too, and the 600 is bought with false alarms whose count the model can report but whose cost only the business can price. A threshold change is therefore a decision about which side of that trade to sit on.

questions.learningObjective: compute an area under a threshold curve by counting pairwise orderings
questions.stem: Ten parcels are scored: four are late with scores 0.9, 0.7, 0.4 and 0.1, and six are on time with scores 0.8, 0.6, 0.3, 0.2, 0.05 and 0.01. Counting a tie as half a win, what is the area under this model's curve of false-positive against true-positive rate?
questions.explanation: There are 4 × 6 = 24 late-on-time pairs, and the area is the share of them the model orders correctly. The score of 0.9 outranks all 6 on-time scores, 0.7 outranks 5, 0.4 outranks 4, and 0.1 outranks 2, so 6 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 17 pairs are won and 17 ÷ 24 = 0.708333. The independent route builds the curve itself, walking the scores down in order and recording the two rates after each: 0.25 at no false positives, 0.25 at one sixth, 0.5 at one sixth, 0.5 at a third, 0.75 at a third, 0.75 at two thirds, 0.75 at half, 1.0 at half, and 1.0 at five sixths, and the trapezoids between those points add to the same 0.708333.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute the false alarms implied by a perfect-recall threshold
questions.stem: A network sees 1,000 parcels a day, of which 3 percent, or 30, arrive late. A team wants a model that flags every late parcel, whatever number of false alarms that requires. How many on-time parcels will be dragged into the manual check along with them?
questions.explanation: Catching all 30 late parcels at a precision of 0.03 means the flagged group is 30 ÷ 0.03 = 1,000 cases, so the false alarms number 1,000 − 30 = 970. The independent route uses the base rate: 3 percent of 1,000 is 30 late parcels and 97 percent is 970 on time, and a model with no misses at all must flag every one of those 970, because each is a case it says yes to. That is the arithmetic behind the phrase catch everything, and it is why perfection on a rare outcome is never available: the volume of the review is set by how common the outcome is, not by how good the model is.

questions.learningObjective: compute a total squared error from a prediction table
questions.stem: A model predicts delivery times of 10, 20 and 30 hours where the recorded times were 12, 20 and 24. What is the total squared error over those three cases?

questions.stem: Each tree in a forest is grown on a bootstrap sample of 1,000 rows drawn with replacement from a table of 1,000. Roughly what share of those 1,000 rows is left out of a given tree's sample, and so available for scoring that tree on its own?
questions.explanation: A given row is left out when every one of the 1,000 draws misses it, and each draw misses it with probability 999/1000, so the share left out is 1 − (999/1000)^1000 = 1 − 0.3677 = 0.6323. The independent route replaces the finite product by its limit: for a large sample the same quantity is 1 − 1/e, and with 1/e = 0.36788 that is 0.63212, agreeing to two decimal places. So roughly 632 rows are out of the bag for any one tree, which is how a forest can be scored without a separate reserved sample, at the price of an estimate per tree that is noisier than a proper held-out block would give.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: compute how a later round trades gains for new mistakes
questions.stem: A boosting round leaves 6 errors out of 200 cases and the next round leaves 4. Every one of the second round's 4 errors is a case the first round also got wrong. How many cases that the first round had right did the second round get wrong?
questions.explanation: The first round had 200 − 6 = 194 correct and the second has 200 − 4 = 196, and of the second round's 196 correct answers 4 come from cases the first round had failed, leaving 196 − 4 = 192 that the first round also had right. Broken cases are therefore 194 − 192 = 2. The independent route is the trade itself: the second round fixed 6 − 4 = 2 of the first round's errors and broke 2 of its correct cases, and 2 gained against 2 lost is exactly the net rise of 2 in the correct count, which agrees with 194 rising to 196. Boosting is therefore not a monotone improvement, and a round that raises the score is still capable of reversing cases that were previously right.
questions.hint: Work out how many correct cases each round had, then subtract the ones the second round took from previously wrong cases.

The model is well matched at every capacity, since both errors fall or stay close at each of the three settings

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a squared loss chases one bad case
questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism by which a squared loss is captured by its largest error
questions.stem: Explain why a squared training loss is dominated by its largest error, what that does to the shape of the fitted model, and when that behaviour is the right one.

answer.exemplar: The loss adds up squared gaps, and squaring makes cost grow faster than the error, so a miss of twenty hours is charged four hundred while a miss of one hour is charged one. A single such case therefore outweighs a hundred ordinary misses, and a fit that minimises the total spends much of its effort on that row: it will bend towards it even when the bend damages every other case, and the resulting line is pulled towards the extreme rather than towards the general run of the data. Two things follow about the shape. The fitted model becomes sensitive to which rows happen to be in the sample, since removing one of them changes the answer materially, and the residuals on ordinary cases are worse than a less aggressive fit would make them. When this is correct is a question about the world and not about method: if twenty hours of delay genuinely destroys a parcel while two hours is a nuisance, the quadratic cost is an accurate description of the harm and the fit is doing its job. If the extreme is a keying error or a warehouse fire, the same property is a defect, and an absolute loss, which charges twenty for twenty and one for one, is the better description of what the business actually loses.

questions.explanation: The dominance is arithmetic before it is statistical, and it propagates straight into the fitted parameters because the procedure is defined by minimising that total. It also has a sampling consequence that is easy to miss: with a loss that grows faster than linearly, the fit is not just less accurate but less stable, since the identity of a single extreme row can move the answer more than a hundred ordinary rows do, so two samples from the same population can produce visibly different models. That instability is the strongest practical argument for an absolute loss on ordinary data, since a loss that treats every miss in proportion to its size is far less hostage to which rows were collected.
questions.hint: Ask how the cost of a miss changes as the miss grows, and then what a fit minimising that total is obliged to do about the row that produced it.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a single combined score hides
questions.learningObjective: explain the assumption a single combined classification score embeds
questions.stem: Explain what a single combined classification score assumes about the two kinds of mistake, and say what a reader should ask for instead when that assumption does not hold.

answer.exemplar: Combining two rates into one requires weighting them, and a harmonic mean weights them equally while refusing to let either be rescued by being large. That is a real claim rather than a neutral summary: it asserts that a false alarm and a genuine miss cost about the same. It also has a second, subtler consequence, because the combination moves least when the two rates are close and moves most when they diverge, so a model that is excellent on one rate and poor on the other is pushed towards a middling figure that describes neither of its behaviours. When the assumption does not hold, the reader should ask for the two rates separately, and for the counts behind them. The counts are what turn a rate into a decision: a share of flagged cases that are genuine at 0.90 means something quite different when forty cases are flagged than when forty thousand are, and a share of frauds found at 0.30 means something different again when there are twenty frauds in the period. The correct summary for an asymmetric cost is therefore not a cleverer single number but a pair of rates with their denominators, plus the threshold that produced them, since the threshold is what connects the pair to the volume of work the decision creates.

questions.explanation: The reason combined scores are so widely used is that one figure is easy to report and easy to trend, and the cost of that convenience is that a genuine weighting decision has been made implicitly and cannot be inspected. Anyone reading such a figure should ask two questions: what ratio of costs does this combination assume, and what are the counts behind the two rates it was built from. A single figure answers neither, and a figure that cannot be interrogated is a figure that cannot be disagreed with, which is why the more informative practice is to publish the rates and the volume and let the reader apply their own cost. That is not pedantry, because the same 0.80 is a good result and a poor one depending entirely on how many cases the decision applies to.
questions.hint: Ask what ratio of costs the combination assumes, and what the counts behind the two rates would add.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a model card is for
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose and limits of a model card
questions.stem: Explain what a model card is for, which of its contents do the most work, and why the subgroup figures on it matter more than the headline.

answer.exemplar: A model card is the document that tells a reader what a model is for, what it was measured on, and where its measurements stop being applicable, so that a person deciding whether to rely on it can do so without access to the people who built it. The contents that do the most work are the least glamorous: the stated purpose and the population it was evaluated on, the subgroup breakdown, the known failure modes, and the conditions under which the team intends to revisit it. The headline figure is the least useful entry, because a single correct-case rate on a large block can be produced by a strong model on most of the traffic and a poor one on the rest, and a reader who is deciding about a rural route or a low-value order cannot extract that from the headline. Two rates of 0.95 on forty-two thousand cases and 0.75 on eight thousand reconcile perfectly to a headline of 0.92, so the breakdown adds nothing to the arithmetic and everything to the decision. The second thing a card should carry is the date and the data period, because a card without them is a snapshot whose figures expire silently, and a model whose inputs have since drifted will still be described by the number that was true when the card was written. Finally, a card should name the cases where the model should not be used at all, since a model that is only ever described by what it can do invites application to the cases it cannot handle.

questions.explanation: A model card exists to move the knowledge of why a number is what it is out of the heads of the team that built the model and into the hands of the people who will use it, which is the only way a later reader can tell whether it applies to their case. Its most valuable sections are the ones that constrain rather than advertise, namely the population the evaluation covered, the subgroup figures, the known failure modes and the review date. The headline rate is the least informative line on the card precisely because it is the one most likely to be quoted out of context, and the subgroup figures earn their place by showing where the headline's average is being carried. A card with no review date is worse than none in one respect, because it lends a stale number the authority of a documented one.
questions.hint: Ask which section of such a document constrains a reader rather than advertising the model, and why the headline rate is the least useful one.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a holdout can be read once
questions.learningObjective: explain why repeated use of a holdout destroys its value
questions.stem: Explain why a holdout stops being a holdout the first time it is used to make a decision, and say what a team should do instead when it needs to try many settings.

answer.exemplar: A holdout is valuable for exactly one property, which is that nothing was decided using it, and that property is consumed by any decision that reads it. Compare thirty settings on 200 cases and take the best, and the reported figure is the maximum of thirty draws from that sample rather than a single draw, so it sits above what the chosen setting will achieve on the next 200 cases by an amount that depends on how many settings were tried and not on how many cases the block held. One model scoring 0.80 and a best-of-thirty figure of 0.92 differ by twenty-four cases, and every one of those is a case the block was used to select on. Enlarging the block does not repair this, since a larger block steadies the estimate without removing the bias, which is the mistake that makes an expensive re-run feel like a solution. The correct arrangement is to set the holdout aside, use cross-validation on the remaining rows to make every choice, and read the holdout exactly once at the end. When a search must be run more than once, for instance after new data arrives, the honest move is to reserve a fresh block rather than to re-read the old one, and to report the earlier figure as what it was: a measurement of that block rather than a forecast for the next one.

questions.explanation: The asymmetry is between decisions and measurements, and it is easy to overlook because reading a holdout feels like measuring it. A measurement reports what a block contains; a decision selects using what a block contains, and once the selection has been made the block's contents have contributed to the model in a way that no arithmetic can undo. The inflation is not proportional to the block size but to the number of tries, so a team that has compared thirty settings cannot recover honesty by scoring one more block, only by reserving one. This is also why the practice of repeatedly checking a production score and adjusting when it looks bad is the same error at a larger scale, and why the fix is procedural rather than statistical.
questions.hint: Ask what the reported figure becomes once a block has been searched over, and what growing the block would and would not fix.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: explain distribution shift and the cheapest ways to detect it
questions.stem: Explain what distribution shift is, why a model can be correct about the world and still degrade, and which two cheap checks detect it before the outcome score moves.

answer.exemplar: A fitted model encodes relationships estimated over a particular population and a particular period, and distribution shift is the arrival of cases from a different population or a different period. The model is not wrong about the world; it is answering a question about a world it was not shown, which is why degradation can be substantial while every weight in the model remains exactly as fitted. The first cheap check is a comparison of input summaries against the training period, the mean, the spread, the share of missing values and the share of values outside the documented range for each input, none of which needs a label and all of which move first. The second is a comparison of the class mix, since a base rate that falls from ten percent to two will collapse the rate of genuine catches among the flagged cases even when the ordering of cases is unchanged, and that single change is enough to make a model look broken. Both checks are summaries, which is their limitation: they show that the inputs have moved without showing which cases the model now gets wrong. The confirmation therefore has to be a score on freshly labelled data, gathered at the real prediction moment, and the practical order is to confirm the fall first, then look at the input summaries, then go and find what in the business changed, since a shift of that size almost always has an explanation that also suggests what else may have moved with it.

questions.explanation: The reason this failure mode is under-handled is that nothing about the model announces it. The code is unchanged, the threshold is unchanged, the saved parameters are unchanged, and every automated test continues to pass, so the only evidence available is a comparison against the period the model was fitted on, which is why recording those summaries at training time is what makes the comparison possible later. The two checks are cheap because both are computed on inputs alone and need no outcome, and they are early because the inputs are what change first: a new upstream system, a new customer mix, a seasonal peak, a policy change. The honest limit of both is that a summary can be unchanged while the joint distribution has moved, so they raise suspicion rather than measure damage, and the damage is quantified only by a score on data labelled after the shift.
questions.hint: Ask what is unchanged when the model degrades, and which comparisons can be made without waiting for a single label.

questions.subject: DATA_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Fixing the metric before the work
questions.learningObjective: explain why a metric chosen after seeing results cannot be trusted
questions.stem: Explain why the metric has to be chosen before the work rather than after, and say what a team should write down first in order to choose one honestly.

answer.exemplar: A metric chosen after the results are in is not a measurement, it is a summary of whichever model happened to be built, and it will be whichever metric makes that model look best. A team that tries three models on an overall correct-case rate and then reports the rate at which each one finds the cases that matter has learned nothing about the second figure and has learned a great deal about how to choose a flattering one. The tell is that the metric changes between the interim update and the final report, and a second tell is that the metric is one whose value nobody had to think about in advance. What should be written down first is the decision the model serves, the two errors it can make, and what each of those costs in the same units. A fraud review where a miss costs fifty times a false alarm has a very different headline from a review where the ratio is one to five, and the same fitted model can be the right choice in one and the wrong choice in the other. With the costs fixed, the metric follows rather than being negotiated, and the threshold can then be set by asking which operating point makes the expected cost lowest. Fixing the metric first also removes a quieter temptation, which is redefining the problem after the fact when the model turns out to be unable to solve it, and the discipline of a written-down metric is what makes that visible.

questions.explanation: The argument is not primarily about honesty, though it is that too, and it is about the fact that a metric selected after the fact carries no information about the problem. It describes the models that were built rather than the decision that has to be made, and two teams with identical data can therefore report identical-sounding figures while having measured entirely different things. Writing down the decision and the cost of each error first makes the choice of metric a deduction rather than a preference, and it forces two questions that are otherwise skipped: which of the two errors is scarce, and what volume of work the operating point creates. Those two answers determine the threshold as well as the headline, so deciding them early is what stops a team from discovering its own cost structure after it has committed.
questions.hint: Ask what a metric chosen after the fact describes, and what has to be written down before the choice of metric becomes a deduction.

The untouched block comes last, once, and it is the only figure in the process that forecasts performance on cases nobody has seen. Pooling the ten fold scores into one number before looking at the spread throws away precisely that evidence.

questions.learningObjective: order the steps that turn a cost ratio into an operating point
questions.stem: A team must fix one operating threshold for a model that will be deployed unchanged. Put these four steps in the order that produces a threshold someone can defend.

options.text: Write down what a false alarm costs and what a miss costs, expressed in the same units
Convert each candidate threshold into counts of false alarms and of missed cases on recent data
Price each candidate at those costs and discard the ones another candidate beats on both counts
Fix the chosen threshold, and publish the two rates and the case volume it produces

questions.explanation: The costs come first because without them there is nothing to compare and the choice degenerates into a preference about which rate looks better. Converting candidates to counts comes second and is the step that makes the comparison real, since a rate of 0.90 among flagged cases means something entirely different when forty cases are flagged than when forty thousand are. Pricing and discarding third is where a setting can be eliminated without any judgement, since a threshold that is beaten on both the number of false alarms and the number of misses is dominated whatever the ratio. Publishing last matters as much as choosing, because the rates and the volume together are what let a later reader check whether the cost ratio has changed, and a fixed threshold with unrecorded rates cannot be re-examined when it does.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be known before the candidate thresholds can be compared at all, and what must be recorded so the choice can be revisited.
